title: Still Talking Work on WeChat? Alibaba and Tencent Both Want to Lead You Into a New Market
excerpt: Productivity tools, enterprise social networking — lukewarm ideas that are getting attention again now that Alibaba and Tencent are pouring money in
body:
Productivity tools, enterprise social networking — lukewarm ideas that are getting attention again now that Alibaba and Tencent are pouring money in

By [WeChat's own account](http://tech.qq.com/a/20151023/057238.htm#p=1), 570 million Chinese users cannot get through a day without it, from the moment they wake up to the moment they fall asleep. As you have probably noticed, a good share of that time goes to handling your boss and your colleagues.

Now China's two largest internet companies want to pull that part of your time out of WeChat.

At a launch event late last month, DingTalk, Alibaba's workplace social tool, said it had signed up 1.5 million registered companies — and it had gone so far as to put taunting ads in the subway station outside Tencent's front door.

Little more than a year ago, DingTalk was a minor, unremarkable product inside Alibaba Group. In its first version, uploading a profile photo would warp it.

On the other side, WeCom, already in testing at a fair number of companies for two months, launched on April 18.

Once a company applies to switch WeCom on, its employees can log in straight away with their WeChat accounts. The name suggests what it may become: a second WeChat, for work only.

## Chinese Companies Have Always Wanted to Make You More Efficient. None Has Ever Caught On

In the United States, IT services that speed up communication inside a company are a big market. [By VisionMobile's count](http://www.visionmobile.com/product/business-productivity-apps/), apps of this kind were worth $28 billion in 2013 and were expected to reach $58 billion in 2016.

Several companies have gone public on Nasdaq on nothing more than making other businesses more efficient. Salesforce, worth over $50 billion, sells CRM — customer relationship management — software; Microsoft, worth nearly $400 billion, runs collaboration services of its own, among them SharePoint, Skype and OneDrive.

There are several private giants too. Slack, which set out to replace email, was worth $4 billion two and a half years after it was founded. Zenefits, which handles human resources, took only two years to pass a $4.5 billion valuation.

More of them have simply sold themselves to a larger company for a high price. Microsoft alone bought three such apps — Sunrise, Wunderlist and Acompli — each said to have cost more than $100 million.

And there are more of them every year. Since 2008, [among the companies applying to the incubator Y Combinator](http://themacro.com/articles/2016/05/the-startup-zeitgeist/), the number whose business model is paid online software has quadrupled. This year it has already overtaken advertising.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702111932GbDue07cVsH3Ekym.jpg-w600)

In China, the most recent listing of this kind you are likely to have heard of is still Kingsoft, founded by Qiu Bojun, going public in Hong Kong in 2007. Today the company makes nearly twice as much from online games as it does from office software.

China is not short of homegrown office collaboration software. For every popular American business productivity app, there is a Chinese imitator.

- Document collaboration, like Google Docs: Yiqixie, Shimo;
- Team chat, like Slack: Banliao, Worktile, Pubu IM;
- Project collaboration, like Basecamp: Teambition, Tower.im, Fengche

But going by what these startups have disclosed about their funding, raising money has not been easy.

- Shimo Docs: founded September 2014, raised an 8 million yuan angel round that December.
- Tower.im: founded 2012, a Series A of several million dollars in January 2013, a Series A+ of several million dollars in August 2015
- Teambition: founded April 2011, an angel round in June 2013, a $5 million Series A in 2014, a $12 million Series B in September 2015

On their own the numbers look respectable. Set against the consumer market, the money is small and it arrives slowly.

Ele.me's Series D alone, in January 2015, was worth more than everything the companies above raised put together. Subsidizing customers on that scale is hard to keep up, yet the money kept arriving round after round — which tells you where capital's preferences lie.

## The Gap in Enthusiasm Comes Down to Habit

The difference between the Chinese and American markets begins with what users are used to.

In the American market, office collaboration tools have been part of many people's jobs for years. Take email, the most basic of them: [according to Pew's 2011 data](http://www.pewinternet.org/2012/06/06/main-report-15/), 59% of American adults typically use it every day. Even among people over 65, 48% do.

Once the habit of using a dedicated tool is there, other tools built for work go down easily.

China has no such foundation. When Steve Jobs started Apple in 1976, China was in the last year of the Cultural Revolution. By the end of 1980, when Bill Gates had already made a PC on every desk an irreversible trend, China was still pushing through market reforms.

Outside foreign firms and internet companies, plenty of Chinese companies still do not use corporate email.

Digital collaboration tools spread in China long ago. It used to be QQ; now it is mostly WeChat. Assigning tasks, keeping in touch with colleagues, keeping in touch with clients, sending and storing files, holding meetings online — all of it can be settled there.

Without anyone intending it, these tools have improved the way companies communicate: inefficient communication still beats none.

Working through WeChat has its costs. Moments and all those official accounts can break your concentration at any moment and drag your output down. And on your own time, one message about work can ruin your mood.

## The Market Has Finally Got Its Giants

Alibaba had tried plenty of chat apps before this: Zhangshang Wangxin, Hupan, Laiwang, and Alipay after its 9.0 upgrade. Most people have probably never heard of any of those chat features.

In October 2014, a year after launch, Laiwang still had not caught on. It hovered around 40th to 50th on the App Store's social app chart. Alibaba had already put a great deal into it: the product and engineering team alone ran to 200 people, DingTalk's founder Chen Hang among them.

Seeing no future in Laiwang, Chen Hang took six people and set out to build a new app on his own, looking for an opening in the enterprise market. DingTalk launched in early 2015. At that point Chen Hang positioned it as nothing more than a chat app for companies, something set apart from WeChat.

With version 2.0 in May, DingTalk took on a second job as an office collaboration tool. By building an open platform, the team meant to pull every kind of business productivity tool in the field into its own app. The first batch came from established vendors such as Hechuang, Lanling, Fanwei and Tower, and DingTalk said it would put 1 billion yuan into a fund to support developers.

To push DingTalk, Alibaba worked harder than it had before. An industry insider who also builds enterprise communication tools told QDaily, half in jest, that during that stretch Chen Hang "made the rounds" of every startup in Hangzhou, large or small — so thoroughly that finding a customer of their own kept getting harder.

They also ran ads in airports, on high-speed trains and in office-building elevators. Advertising spending last autumn alone is said to have reached [500 million yuan](http://www.time-weekly.com/html/20160503/33253_1.html). DingTalk said at the time that it would also give employees of certified companies benefits and subsidies worth 200 million yuan.

Neither mass offline advertising nor subsidies are common in the enterprise market. The people who decide whether to use a product are usually a company's senior managers, and reaching them by those channels is both slow and a waste of money.

In January this year Wang Hao, the Xiami founder who runs Alibaba's music business, joined DingTalk as vice president for business development — a measure of how seriously Alibaba's leadership takes the product.

The blunt, aggressive approach worked in the end. Alibaba's 2015 annual report put the number of certified companies on DingTalk at 1 million by the end of last year. For the past six months it has held first place on the App Store's business chart almost without a break.

Challenged by a social product, Tencent should by rights feel little pressure. It is good at building social products, and it already owns the complete web of relationships built up in QQ and WeChat.

But WeCom did badly after launch. Within a week it slid from 86th to 531st on the App Store chart, and in the business category it ranked far below DingTalk.

![WeCom's iOS download ranking fell fast after launch. Data: AppAnnie](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702111933PWDo6yNVs7FrmILU.jpg-w600)

The newly launched WeCom can be read as Tencent's answer to DingTalk. It is not a very serious answer.

You can see that in the team itself. Both sit inside the WeChat business group, but the people who built WeCom are not the WeChat app's developers; they are the group that used to run Tencent's corporate email.

That team had also built WeChat Contact Book and WeRead, and many of its staff were pulled over from WeRead.

WeCom looks a great deal like WeChat in many places. It is nonetheless a program written from scratch — the WeChat app's team did not share its code, and when the developers hit a problem they had to go across teams and sort it out informally.

It is not hard to see why Tencent has not thrown everything at enterprise services. WeChat has become an app that handles every online need a user has. The longer someone stays in WeCom, the less time they spend in WeChat.

And the advertising that runs inside WeChat is hard to fit into an enterprise service. If WeCom works too well, WeChat's ad business is bound to suffer.

[Advertising matters enormously to Tencent's future revenue](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/24086.html). It passed games as the company's fastest-growing business back in 2014, and in each of last year's final three quarters its revenue doubled. In 2015, ads on mobile QQ Zone, WeChat official accounts and Moments brought in 17.5 billion yuan.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702111933V3u1A8LYHW6cGgvy.jpg-w600)

After WeChat itself, WeCom is the second Tencent app that requires the company to cannibalize its own business. Until that bind is resolved, WeCom is unlikely to be a match for DingTalk, which has Alibaba behind it in full.

## What Will DingTalk and WeCom Change?

Even without Alibaba and Tencent, enterprise collaboration tools would probably have become the next corner of the internet business to draw attention.

Most products aimed at ordinary consumers have matured in recent years, and there is less and less ground left unexplored. The main services — social networking, e-commerce, ride-hailing, food delivery — have been divided up among the giants. Life keeps getting harder for new companies, and investors can no longer count on stumbling into the next hundred- or thousand-fold return.

The enterprise market, though, is still ground nobody has fully broken.

On the other hand, now that everyone is used to phone apps, chat tools like WeChat above all, learning an office collaboration app is no great leap.

Then DingTalk arrived and pushed that habit further. Alibaba's marketing may lead more people to see that work talk and private life should be kept apart, and to expect more of their own working hours.

The giants' arrival has also changed how founders see this market. Fenxiang Xiaoke, originally a CRM company, announced in March that it was turning into a mobile office platform — remaking a product built for salespeople into a communication and collaboration tool almost any office worker could use. On its own website it compares itself directly to WeCom, to help visitors grasp what it does.

For small and mid-sized companies, the office market is also an easier place to make money. An internet service for consumers usually has to gather tens of millions, even a hundred million, users before profit is worth discussing.

In the enterprise market, as soon as one company starts using your service it may pay you directly for the efficiency it gains. "Business owners are more willing than individual consumers to pay for what they need," Chen Leihua, CEO of Coremail, which builds custom corporate email for specific industries, told QDaily.

In the United States, far smaller user bases already hold up whole business models. When Zenefits passed a $4.5 billion valuation, only 100,000 people had bought health insurance through it. A year after Slack launched it had just 268,000 daily active users, but more than 70,000 of them paid.

This is a virtuous circle. As more companies take these office collaboration products up and pay for them, the products get the chance to improve, which draws more people in.

Since the giants arrived, some fairly large companies have begun using their services. Toutiao, for one.

Toutiao had considered overseas services before, but ruled them out each time over performance and network stability.

"Even with DingTalk, we spent close to a year looking at it and gradually widening the trial before we finally decided to adopt it," said Xie Xin, the company's vice president of human resources.

Bigger companies are careful in the early stages of deciding on a product like this. The more such large customers one wins, the better it can show what it is worth. Fosun Group, Focus Media and Zhonggong Education are all DingTalk users at the moment.

Whether or not DingTalk or WeCom finally comes out on top, the fight will make more people see that they do not have to cram everything into WeChat.

With that change, companies across the industry may find new openings.
